```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
```

## Data load and preparation before modelling

```{r read_data}
gss16 <- read.csv("data/gss16.csv")

gss16_advfront <- gss16 %>%
  select(advfront, emailhr, educ, polviews, wrkstat) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(
    advfront = case_when(
      advfront == "Strongly agree" ~ "Agree",
      advfront == "Agree" ~ "Agree",
      TRUE ~ "Not agree"
    ),
    advfront = factor(advfront) %>% fct_relevel("Not agree", "Agree"),
    polviews = case_when(
      str_detect(polviews, "[Cc]onservative") ~ "Conservative",
      str_detect(polviews, "[Ll]iberal") ~ "Liberal",
      TRUE ~ polviews
    ),
    polviews = factor(polviews) %>% fct_relevel("Conservative", "Moderate", "Liberal"),
    wrkstat = factor(wrkstat)
  )
glimpse(gss16_advfront)
```

## Exercise 1: Create a linear regression model

### a) Fit and interpret the simple linear regression

```{r ex1-model}
model_1 <- lm(emailhr ~ educ, data = gss16_advfront)
summary(model_1)
broom::tidy(model_1, conf.int = TRUE)
broom::glance(model_1)
```

The fitted line is **emailhr = `r round(coef(model_1)[1], 2)` + `r round(coef(model_1)[2], 2)` × educ**. The slope means that each additional year of education is associated with an estimated `r round(coef(model_1)[2], 2)`-hour change in weekly email time on average. This is an association, not a causal effect.

### b) Model performance and assumptions

```{r ex1-diagnostics}
g1 <- broom::glance(model_1)
rmse_1 <- sqrt(mean(residuals(model_1)^2))
model_1_metrics <- tibble(R_squared = g1$r.squared, Adjusted_R_squared = g1$adj.r.squared, RMSE = rmse_1)
model_1_metrics

aug_1 <- broom::augment(model_1)
ggplot(aug_1, aes(.fitted, .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Fitted weekly email hours", y = "Residuals", title = "Residuals versus fitted values") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(aug_1, aes(sample = .std.resid)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.35) + stat_qq_line(colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q plot of standardised residuals") + theme_minimal()
```

R-squared is `r round(g1$r.squared, 3)` and RMSE is `r round(rmse_1, 2)` hours; R-squared is the fraction of sample variation explained, while RMSE gives a typical residual scale in hours. Use the residual plots to assess assumptions: a roughly pattern-free residual cloud with similar spread supports linearity and constant variance, and points near the Q-Q line support approximately normal errors. Email hours are often skewed and may contain extreme values, so departures in the plots and the modest explanatory power mean this simple model should be treated as a rough summary rather than a precise predictor.

## Exercise 2: Compare two linear models

```{r ex2-model}
model_2 <- lm(emailhr ~ educ + advfront, data = gss16_advfront)
broom::tidy(model_2, conf.int = TRUE)
broom::glance(model_2)

comparison <- tibble(
  Model = c("educ only", "educ + advfront"),
  R_squared = c(broom::glance(model_1)$r.squared, broom::glance(model_2)$r.squared),
  Adjusted_R_squared = c(broom::glance(model_1)$adj.r.squared, broom::glance(model_2)$adj.r.squared),
  RMSE = c(sqrt(mean(residuals(model_1)^2)), sqrt(mean(residuals(model_2)^2))),
  AIC = c(AIC(model_1), AIC(model_2))
)
comparison
```

In the second model, the `r round(coef(model_2)["advfrontAgree"], 2)` coefficient for **Agree** is the adjusted difference in predicted weekly email hours between respondents who agree and those who do not, at the same education level. The reference group is Not agree. Compare models on the same data: higher adjusted R-squared and lower RMSE/AIC indicate better in-sample fit (AIC also penalises extra parameters). Here, the model with advfront `r if (comparison$RMSE[2] < comparison$RMSE[1]) "has a lower RMSE" else "does not have a lower RMSE"`; any improvement is an association and need not be practically large.

## Exercise 3: Create a workflow to fit a model to the training data

```{r split-data}
set.seed(1234)
gss16_split <- initial_split(gss16_advfront, prop = 0.75, strata = advfront)
gss16_train <- training(gss16_split)
gss16_test <- testing(gss16_split)
table(gss16_train$advfront)
table(gss16_test$advfront)
```

### a) Recipe, model and workflow

The outcome has two categories, so logistic regression is appropriate: it models the probability of agreement and returns probabilities between zero and one. Education is numeric, so it can enter the model directly.

```{r ex3-workflow}
gss16_rec_1 <- recipe(advfront ~ educ, data = gss16_train)
gss16_mod_1 <- logistic_reg() %>% set_engine("glm") %>% set_mode("classification")
gss16_wflow_1 <- workflow() %>% add_recipe(gss16_rec_1) %>% add_model(gss16_mod_1)
gss16_fit_1 <- fit(gss16_wflow_1, data = gss16_train)
gss16_pred_1 <- predict(gss16_fit_1, new_data = gss16_test, type = "prob") %>%
  bind_cols(gss16_test %>% select(advfront))
head(gss16_pred_1)
roc_1 <- roc_curve(gss16_pred_1, truth = advfront, .pred_Agree, event_level = "second")
autoplot(roc_1) + labs(title = "ROC curve: education only") + theme_minimal()
```

## Exercise 4: Performance of a logistic regression

### a) Confusion matrix, sensitivity and specificity at 0.83

```{r ex4-cutoff}
cutoff <- 0.83
pred_class_1 <- factor(if_else(gss16_pred_1$.pred_Agree >= cutoff, "Agree", "Not agree"),
                        levels = levels(gss16_test$advfront))
confusion_1 <- table(Predicted = pred_class_1, Actual = gss16_test$advfront)
confusion_1
tn <- confusion_1["Not agree", "Not agree"]
fp <- confusion_1["Agree", "Not agree"]
fn <- confusion_1["Not agree", "Agree"]
tp <- confusion_1["Agree", "Agree"]
confusion_counts <- tibble(Measure = c("True positives", "True negatives", "False positives", "False negatives"), Count = c(tp, tn, fp, fn))
confusion_counts
sensitivity_1 <- tp / (tp + fn)
specificity_1 <- tn / (tn + fp)
tibble(Sensitivity = sensitivity_1, Specificity = specificity_1)
```

Sensitivity is the proportion of actual Agree responses identified as Agree; specificity is the proportion of actual Not agree responses identified as Not agree. The chosen high threshold can reduce false positives while missing more true positives.

### b) Expanded logistic regression workflow

```{r ex4-workflow}
gss16_rec_2 <- recipe(advfront ~ polviews + wrkstat + emailhr + educ, data = gss16_train) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())
gss16_mod_2 <- logistic_reg() %>% set_engine("glm") %>% set_mode("classification")
gss16_wflow_2 <- workflow() %>% add_recipe(gss16_rec_2) %>% add_model(gss16_mod_2)
gss16_fit_2 <- fit(gss16_wflow_2, data = gss16_train)
gss16_pred_2 <- predict(gss16_fit_2, new_data = gss16_test, type = "prob") %>%
  bind_cols(gss16_test %>% select(advfront))
roc_2 <- roc_curve(gss16_pred_2, truth = advfront, .pred_Agree, event_level = "second")
autoplot(roc_2) + labs(title = "ROC curve: expanded model") + theme_minimal()
auc_1 <- roc_auc(gss16_pred_1, truth = advfront, .pred_Agree, event_level = "second")$.estimate
auc_2 <- roc_auc(gss16_pred_2, truth = advfront, .pred_Agree, event_level = "second")$.estimate
tibble(Model = c("Education only", "Expanded predictors"), AUC = c(auc_1, auc_2))
```

AUC summarises discrimination across all possible cutoffs; 0.5 is chance ranking and 1 is perfect ranking. Model `r if (auc_2 > auc_1) "2 has" else if (auc_2 < auc_1) "1 has" else "both have the same"` higher test AUC (`r round(max(auc_1, auc_2), 3)` versus `r round(min(auc_1, auc_2), 3)`), so it performs better by this metric on this test split. The difference is descriptive and may vary across splits; the held-out test set gives a more honest comparison than training performance.
